title: Why Tsunoda feels ‘like a rookie’ for Racing Bulls return
excerpt:
When Yuki Tsunoda was told he would be driving for Racing Bulls at the Dutch Grand Prix, he was on holiday on a beach in Greece and had to rush to prepare for the outing at Zandvoort. He felt so unprepared that he approached the weekend like a rookie.

By the time the Italian Grand Prix came around, Tsunoda had already been working in the simulator in case Isack Hadjar remained sidelined. Despite having a race weekend in the car under his belt and more time to prepare, he still feels like a rookie given the complexity of energy deployment at Monza.

“It was actually yesterday,” Tsunoda said on Thursday when asked when he had learned the news. “I was in the sim just in case. I really didn't know until mid-afternoon, and I heard in the middle of the session. ‘OK, I’m going to drive, so I’ll keep doing the simulator work as I would in a race week.’”

Zandvoort went about as well as could have been expected, given Tsunoda’s unfamiliarity with the car and the demands of a Sprint weekend. After finishing a solid P11, he received positive feedback from Team Principal Alan Permane.

“[It was] positive for sure,” the Japanese racer confirmed. “And even after the debrief, I said, ‘Good luck this season, I enjoyed it,’ or something. Alan said, ‘We might need you again – we might need you again next week. So be prepared.’

“I could tell that I felt some more trust from him after that race. If I did really bad, and anything can happen with this world, maybe I wouldn't get called to drive this week. So yeah, I think this was very positive.”

Although final confirmation came late, Tsunoda had spent the days after Zandvoort assuming he might be needed. He therefore focused on training, working with the Faenza engineers and running in the simulator.

“I was pretty much really chilled, like a usual race week. I was more prepared, I would say, than the week before in the Netherlands, because it all happened suddenly, and now after Isack was injured, I was more prepared.

Lawson to replace Hadjar again at Red Bull in Monza

“So that was probably the healthiest one week I spent in 2026 so far! So yeah, I was really prepared. I'm feeling more ready than ever.”

The biggest challenge now is energy deployment around Monza, an area where Tsunoda lacks the race experience of the drivers who have competed throughout this season, taking in the long straights at places like Shanghai and Spa-Francorchamps.

“I think Netherlands was fortunately one of the easiest tracks I would say to manage the energy, and I can say that I was able to adjust to the car pretty smoothly," said Tsunoda.

“But now it's the most difficult track for that energy deployment, and I already experienced in the simulator how different it is, and really kicks in these challenges of these regulations.

“So yeah, the management, brake early or whatever, those things I really have to practice. And in the simulator, it felt really weird, because I know I can drive faster – but you cannot, because otherwise in total lap time, you'll be slow. So that will be the biggest challenge for me.”

Being quick over a single lap is one thing, but Tsunoda must also adjust to the tactical, energy-management battles that were less prominent at Zandvoort.

“I think it will be more challenging in race condition,” he admitted. “Because this kind of strategic, I would say, battle with the energy management with other cars, I didn't do that, and probably other [drivers] know what the car is going to do after they use the battery to overtake or defend. I only know from the simulator, and the Netherlands was probably the least powerful.

“In short runs I would say I'm not worried as much, because you have free practice anyway, so you know what kind of things, and you can only focus on yourself. But in the race, you have to be proactive, right? So that's the only thing that I have to be more prepared for sure than the Netherlands.”

Tsunoda is hoping to take a step forward from Zandvoort, with a place in Q3 and points on Sunday his ideal scenario. However, he knows it will not be easy.

"I will see for FP1 these energy things, how difficult it is. I really don't know. But I think the car pace is good, and we’re bringing an upgrade here, so I am excited to see that.

“I think the Netherlands was more like I just entered the race a bit like a rookie, so I just tried to learn as much as possible. The time was very tight because of the Sprint format.

“I have to practice a lot of things, like energy deployments, and even over one lap to be patient. I would say I feel like I'm a rookie, and I have to try and learn everything, and try to not miss any single thing that the team is instructing me.”

He also has a special reason to want a good result this weekend: “I want to do well here – I’ve never done well here. Out of five years, I have three DNFs, two I didn't even start. So I don't know what's going on with here, but getting this opportunity, hopefully it’s lucky.”

title: Verstappen sets out target for Monza
excerpt:
Max Verstappen has admitted that he and Red Bull “need to be realistic” about their chances at the upcoming Italian Grand Prix, with the Dutchman setting out the aim of “just trying to have a good weekend”.

Verstappen’s home event last time out in Zandvoort ended in disappointing fashion after he suffered a crash at the end of the first lap, putting him out of the running while stand-in team mate Liam Lawson salvaged points for the squad in P7.

Looking ahead to Monza, Verstappen will sit out Free Practice 1 as Ayumu Iwasa gets behind the wheel before he returns to action for FP2 – and while it is a track that he claimed victory at last season, the four-time World Champion is keeping his expectations modest this time around.

“Let's see,” he said of his prospects. “Of course I'm not doing FP1, so we'll see afterwards how the car will be. Trying to get it into a nice window, but at the same time we also need to be realistic, where we are at the moment as a team and how we're performing.

“We’ll just try to have a good weekend. I know it's already going to be very complex with the energy around here, so we just need to try and understand that first and then we'll just see from there where we are in the pecking order.

“Just going off the last few races, I think we just need to be realistic.”

Looking back at the difficult end to what will be the last Dutch Grand Prix, Verstappen conceded that he does not think it would have been a particularly strong outing even if he had been able to continue.

“I would have loved to have completed the race, even though I don’t think it would have been a magic race for us pace-wise,” he explained.

“The whole weekend we were a bit off, and I was not feeling well so all the combinations were not there.

“But I look back at it with a lot of positives – I won races there, we had really great moments with the fans there, so overall it was a crazy experience and I’m very happy that I got to have a home Grand Prix like that.”

title: Why Piastri want answers to a ‘bigger question’ in Monza
excerpt:
Oscar Piastri believes he and McLaren have "got ideas on how we can make things better" ahead of this weekend's Italian Grand Prix, after the Australian has struggled for performance in recent races.

Team mate and reigning World Champion Lando Norris has put McLaren back on top in Formula 1 after winning the two previous races in Hungary and the Netherlands.

Although Piastri fought for the win in the former before retiring, he was noticeably lacking pace compared with Norris at Zandvoort, finishing 32 seconds adrift of the race winner.

The Dutch Grand Prix marked a complete year since Piastri stood on the top step of the podium, having watched his lead in last year's drivers' standings eventually surpassed by Norris.

Speaking on Thursday's media day ahead of the Italian Grand Prix, Piastri admitted that his struggles were not due to one reason specifically, making it harder to rectify.

"I think it's never been the same issue or thing we're chasing every weekend. It's always been slightly different which I think kind of raises a bigger question," he said.

"If it was just one thing we kept struggling with it would, in some ways, be a bit of an easy fix but I think the fact we've kind of found different ways of having difficulty, we've been trying to answer that question.

"And we are getting closer, finding more ideas and ultimately the only way you can really solve it is by trying stuff on track. Not saying that we've gone away and found this problem, we've definitely got ideas on how we can make things better, both from how I drive the car and how we set up the car.

"Hopefully we can find something that works a bit better. I think in Zandvoort, Qualifying was a much bigger step, Lando and I were very close but clearly in the race there was a deficit. That's the area we're trying to work on."

Piastri believes that the new-for-2026 regulations have created a breed of car which he has struggled to adapt to, while bad luck and reliability problems have also played their part.

"There's definitely things that have not been as easy or as comfortable this year compared to last year," he said.

"Some things we can fix quickly, some things we can't. I think these cars in general, the concept is very different, the tyres are quite different.

"There's a lot of things as well that are not necessarily in our control. Also this season not been easy for other reasons, we've had a lot of struggles with reliability or bad luck."

title: Russell expects tow from Antonelli in Monza Qualifying
excerpt:
George Russell has revealed that Mercedes team mate Kimi Antonelli is primed to help him with a tow during Qualifying for the Italian Grand Prix, despite their respective quests for the 2026 world title.

Russell arrives at the Autodromo Nazionale Monza 59 points behind Antonelli in the Drivers’ Championship standings, having claimed two Grand Prix victories to the Italian’s six so far this season.

Antonelli, however, will drop to the back of the grid for his home race due to a full power unit change, ruling him out of pole position contention before the weekend has even started.

That has raised questions over whether Antonelli might be used to support Russell’s own bid for pole by providing a slipstream along one of Monza’s many long straights – in turn giving the Briton a valuable top-speed boost.

Giving his response during Thursday’s media duties, Russell initially smiled, “I hope so”, before explaining that “they offered it” and “we’ll go for it, see if it works” as Qualifying develops.

He continued: “It’s not maybe as powerful as it once was with the wings open in [Straight Mode] the whole time, but we’ll work as a team. That’s how we do things.”

In terms of Antonelli’s impending grid drop having any other impact on his preparations and approach to the weekend, Russell’s take was clear.

“For me, it doesn’t change anything, because I always want to focus on myself, focus on my limitations and the areas I want to improve,” he said.

“I always said it doesn’t matter if I have a seven-time World Champion as my team mate or a rookie. The job is still the same, so my approach will be exactly the same.”

He added: “I think I’m feeling much better since the summer break, and hoping just to continue building on that momentum.

“Of course, we know we’ve got fierce competition at the moment with McLaren and Ferrari bringing upgrades. We’re still on the back foot in terms of bringing these upgrades to the car.

“We know in that interim it’s not going to be as straightforward as it once was, but hoping to fight for pole and the win again.”

Nonetheless, Russell suggested that “any of the top-four teams” have the potential to succeed this weekend – again being quick to highlight McLaren after their back-to-back victories in Hungary and the Netherlands.

“We can say all we want [about the pecking order], but we’ll soon find out,” he commented. “I think there will be a lot of tough competition.

“The momentum is with McLaren right now. Ferrari has upgrades this weekend. We know Red Bull has a strong power unit. So, I honestly think this weekend it could be between any of the top-four teams, but I hope it’s us.”

title: Norris evaluates chances of victory hat-trick in Monza
excerpt:
Lando Norris is optimistic that he can continue his superb form and win the Italian Grand Prix, but was keen to emphasise that McLaren still have plenty to work on when it comes to their place in the pecking order.

After a lacklustre start to the 2026 season, the reigning World Champion finally returned to the top step at the Hungarian Grand Prix, following the achievement with another hard-fought win in the Netherlands to make him the only non-Mercedes driver to claim back-to-back victories so far.

Although Norris has a chance to extend that streak in Monza, he admitted that predicting a result would be a pointless exercise due to how differently the car behaves at each circuit.

Asked how confident he felt about completing the hat-trick of wins, he said: “It's certainly the plan. It's still hard to know, I think we're at the stage where it's hard to predict where we're going to be.

“I think we also don't want to waste time trying to predict these things. We're just focused, working on the stuff that's in our control. I'm doing the same. Clearly in a good place as a whole team at the minute, we know we have things we really have to try and work on and improve and we'll see if we've been able to make any progress into this weekend.

“Looking forward to it, it's another weekend where we want to be hopeful and believe it's possible. We kind of just have to wait and see.

“It's another track where we want to prove things. I wouldn't say it's a bad circuit for us, we've been good here in the past. I think there are still tracks ahead that I'm not looking forward to quite as much. There's still some good high-speed corners here which we want to try and make use of.

“Still a very long season, lots of different types of tracks we still have ahead of us. The goal is to continue the performances we've had lately, but we'll have to see tomorrow how the pace is and see if we can have another good weekend.”

Norris will be further buoyed by his latest contract that will see him remain at McLaren until the end of 2030, becoming the second driver on the grid to commit to a significant long-term deal after Max Verstappen made a similar announcement ahead of his home race.

“I just love where I am, simple as that,” Norris said of the news. “I don't want to change, don't want to be with other people. Don't want to have a reset and work with anyone else. Happy that I'm with people I love to spend time with, create memories.

“They're my family, [the] team I've been with since beginning in F1, and they're also the team that I believe can help me win races and win more championships. For me there's two big reasons, the people and the performance that we have.

“Not everything in life is about performance, I just want to be places that I'm happy and for now, only been with one team and I'm happy with them.”

title: Colapinto grateful for Alpine ‘trust’ amid contract extension
excerpt:
Franco Colapinto has praised the “trust” from Alpine after agreeing a contract extension with the team, ahead of a weekend in which the Argentinian is hoping an upgrade package can give the Enstone-based outfit an advantage over their rivals.

Another piece of the 2027 driver market fell into place when it was recently confirmed that Colapinto will continue to race for the squad next season, forming an unchanged line-up alongside Pierre Gasly.

It comes after a solid start to the campaign for Colapinto, who has scored 19 points and sits in P12 of the Drivers’ Championship.

“I’m very pleased, very happy,” the 23-year-old said of the news during Thursday’s media day at the Italian Grand Prix. “I’m very excited for what's coming and to continue this journey with the team.

“I'm very grateful for the opportunities this last year, and we grew up a lot together, a big family now. We did a lot of steps together as a team, improving the car in many areas, improving the performance of everyone in the team. I’m happy and looking forward to keep it going.”

Colapinto went on to express his gratitude for the opportunity that he was handed by Executive Advisor Flavio Briatore and “the trust since the start”, adding that he is “very happy with the effort of the team, how we improved lately and the steps that we’ve made together as a family”.

The announcement comes as the driver from Buenos Aires prepares to race with an upgrade package in Monza, with the new parts set to go on both Alpine cars after Gasly ran with them last time out in Zandvoort.

“I think Monza is always a track I enjoy driving, aside of having the upgrade or not,” said Colapinto. “With it, I think it's going to be good. Hopefully it's a good track for us – we'll see how it looks on Friday.

“It’s going to be important to keep working and trying to extra everything out of the car in Qualifying.”

Scoring points in the Netherlands has helped Alpine to move closer to Racing Bulls in the battle for P5 of the Teams’ Championship, with the gap now standing at just three points.

“We are really close,” Colapinto conceded. “With the last upgrade we did a very good step in terms of performance and we are closer to them, which was our goal. We were hoping to do a big step and it happened, and the upgrade is working well, but we need to keep working and putting everything together to be in front of them.

“They are fast, Audi is fast as well. They are bringing I think an upgrade here with the rear wing, so they will be a bit faster, but we have trust in the package we have now and hopefully we can extract everything and be in front.”

title: Leclerc targets ‘very special’ Monza weekend with new engine
excerpt:
Charles Leclerc has echoed team mate Lewis Hamilton’s optimism over an engine upgrade that Ferrari will deploy at the Autodromo Nazionale Monza – expressing his hope of delivering another “very special weekend” in front of the Tifosi.

After an initial update in Austria earlier this season, Ferrari have made further changes to their power unit for the Italian Grand Prix, as part of the team’s 2026 ‘ADUO’ (Additional Development and Upgrade Opportunities) allowance.

With Hamilton talking about the possibility of challenging for victory on Ferrari’s home soil earlier in the day, Leclerc shared similar ambitions when he faced the media – as he pushes to claim what would be third win in red at the famous Temple of Speed.

Asked about the engine update, and what he expects it to bring, Leclerc replied: “It will have a bit more power, which is always a good thing. How much more power? Only time will tell.

“I’ll do my best in order to have a very special weekend like in 2019 and 2024, which are probably the best memories I have in racing, together with [the win in] Monaco in 2024.

“But we are against very tough competition and the engine is definitely our weak part. To do a step forward will help us close a little bit the gap to the guys in front.”

However, Leclerc went on to highlight the “perfect execution” that will be required if Ferrari are to triumph for the third time this season – after Hamilton’s win in Barcelona and the Monegasque’s win at Silverstone.

“If there’s one track we can afford to maybe compromise a little bit Qualifying compared to the race, it’s this one,” he said. “However, our job is to make the car faster, and that will be beneficial for Qualifying and the race.

“On a track like this, we expect to have a bit of a harder time because it’s lots of straight lines and we know that this is a bit of a weak point compared to our competitors so far, but I’m still optimistic.

“Silverstone and Spa weren’t meant to be positive for us and we had a good weekend, but by having a perfect execution. We need to target that here.

“We have a new engine, we have new parts on the car, and I hope that helps us to put the others under a bit more pressure.”

As for how much energy he takes from racing in Ferrari’s backyard, Leclerc added: “Italy has always been very special for me. I kind of grew up here through my karting career, I was very much living with my mechanics here, and so I have a very special connection with Italy and the people.

“To be racing with Ferrari in Italy is already a special experience, but even more so for me. I just really hope we can convert all that positive excitement into a victory on Sunday.”

title: Lawson details ‘biggest challenge’ of Red Bull switch
excerpt:
Liam Lawson has explained how having to carry out Italian Grand Prix preparation with both Red Bull and Racing Bulls has proven to be the “biggest challenge” of switching seats, with the news that he would again drive for the former not coming until Wednesday.

Lawson stepped in at the Milton Keynes-based squad last time out in Zandvoort after Isack Hadjar suffered a wrist injury prior to the event, the New Zealander going on to score points with a P7 finish in Sunday’s race.

It was then announced just before the paddock headed to Monza that Hadjar would again sit out the weekend as his rehabilitation continues, meaning that Lawson will drive alongside Max Verstappen at the team for another outing while Yuki Tsunoda gets a second opportunity in Lawson’s place at Racing Bulls.

Asked during Thursday’s media day about when he learned he would be racing for Red Bull again, Lawson responded: “Wednesday. So, for the last week, it's been sort of just waiting to see. Obviously, trying to give Isack the best chance as well for his recovery.

“But, yeah, I think in the back of my mind, I knew that obviously there was still a chance. Obviously, only being on Wednesday, it felt quite late, but we had enough time to still do a simulator session and normal prep for the weekend.”

Quizzed further on which team’s engineers he had been talking with as he carried out his preparation for the weekend, the 24-year-old said: “Both, honestly. I’ve been doing both, just to try and stay ready for both. Obviously, both teams, both cars to know.

“They're very different to drive, so it's not the easiest thing going between the two, even just in the simulator, but that's been the biggest challenge. But it's nice to finally have an answer, from Wednesday, to know that I can basically just put all my focus onto this car.”

Lawson went on to explain that the Red Bull and Racing Bulls cars are different “everywhere”, adding: “Other than the power unit, obviously, they're very different to drive.

“The main thing with the Red Bull, the high-speed grip is probably the most impressive just coming from my car. But the way they drive, the balance of the car is very, very different.

“So, yeah, without saying too much, it is a very different car to drive. Honestly, the feedback I get through the steering, everything, the way it feels, the way it moves around, it's very different.”

Despite the challenge of adapting between the two, Lawson is keen to maximise the opportunity of driving the RB22 again during the weekend ahead at Monza.

“[My mindset is to] just try and make the most of it,” he explained. “Again, I think it's an interesting position for me to be in. Zandvoort was, being a Sprint weekend, obviously quite stressful at times, but overall it was a good weekend.

“And at least now I've had that, it should be a bit easier to adjust. We also have three practice sessions here. It's a much more normal weekend, so, yeah, it's another good opportunity.”

title: Antonelli explains approach to starting at the back in Monza
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli has outlined his mindset as he prepares to start from the back in front of his home crowd at the Italian Grand Prix, with the Mercedes driver also explaining whether he will sacrifice his Qualifying to support team mate George Russell.

Despite arriving at the event with a 59-point lead in the championship, it was confirmed ahead of the weekend that Antonelli will serve a grid penalty at Monza due to a planned engine change, posing an extra challenge for the Italian on Sunday.

However, when speaking to the media on Thursday ahead of his local Grand Prix, Antonelli spoke of the “opportunity” he could take from the circumstances as well as admitting that his grid position helps to alleviate some of the pressure from racing at home.

“It feels very special [to be leading the championship at my home race],” he explained. “Definitely a lot different compared to last year, and I'm very much looking forward to this weekend, despite starting from the back.

“But it's also a big opportunity I have, and very much looking forward to it. I think it's going to be very enjoyable – I will be able to enjoy it much more than what I did previously, and hopefully we can still do a great race.

“I think [starting from the back] in some ways helps to release pressure, although I'd very much rather fight for pole and start there at the front. But in some way it makes me a bit more relaxed going into the weekend. I think also that's why I'm going to be able to enjoy more the driving and the weekend itself.

“And of course it's a different opportunity, it's an opportunity to try something different during the weekend, a different work method as well in Free Practice especially, because we have the chance to do so. So yeah, I think it's going to a very interesting weekend.”

In terms of what he believes might be possible from his starting position, Antonelli said: “In an ideal world, I think realistically top five you can do well, but it's all driven by also your pace, how fast you are, what's the gap between cars.

“We might be really quick, but Ferrari, McLaren or Red Bull, they might be very close [and then] it’s probably not enough to catch them during the race, but we'll see. Definitely I feel very free mentally going into this weekend. I'm actually very excited, very much looking forward to it, but with no real pressure.”

Given his impending penalty, Antonelli was also quizzed on whether he might do anything to support fellow Mercedes driver Russell – such as providing a tow – during Qualifying.

“It has been discussed with the team, and yes, we have agreed on a few things,” the 20-year-old said. “Let's see how the session develops, but if the team will ask me to do so, I will do it.”

Overall, the championship leader conceded that he is carrying a very different mindset into the weekend compared to how he felt one year earlier, having experienced a difficult spell across the European leg of his rookie season.

“[The main change this year is] that I don't have to prove as much as I had to do last year,” Antonelli explained. “Last year, obviously I was coming from a difficult period as well, and I felt like I had to prove myself, to prove that I could belong in F1.

“I feel like also that increased a lot the pressure on myself, and that made me drive very tense. I wasn’t really enjoying as well the time in the car. This year, obviously I'm lucky to have a great car, but as well, also the year of experience makes a huge difference.

“I feel much more mature, much more in control of the situation. And obviously then also when you get the good results in, it's always one less thing to prove and I've proven that I can win, I've proved that I can perform, and that's why coming into this weekend, yes it's my home race, it's great, but it is another race like the others.”

title: Liam Lawson reveals 'quite late' Red Bull call as Isack Hadjar pain persists
excerpt:
Liam Lawson has another chance to show Red Bull just what he can do in Monza.

Liam Lawson has revealed he was told by Red Bull on Wednesday that he would again replace Isack Hadjar, a decision he admitted came "quite late".

Hadjar remains on the sidelines for this weekend's Italian Grand Prix due to persistent wrist pain following an injury sustained while training during the summer break.

As at Zandvoort a fortnight ago, Lawson has been called up from Racing Bulls to replace the Frenchman, while Yuki Tsunoda is again alongside Arvid Lindblad in the sister outfit.

Lawson knew there was a strong chance he would be back in the RB22 at Monza, and he still managed to complete his usual pre-race prep despite the late decision for Hadjar to sit out.

Asked when he was told he would replace Hadjar again, Lawson told select media, including RacingNews365: "Wednesday. So, for the last week, it's been sort of just waiting to see.

"Obviously, trying to give Isack the best chance as well for his recovery. But, yeah, I think in the back of my mind, I knew that obviously there was still a chance.

"But, obviously, only being on Wednesday, it felt quite late, but we had enough time to still do a simulator session and normal prep for the weekend."

Lawson's second chance

Monza represents another chance for Lawson to show Red Bull just what he can do, particularly after impressing in Zandvoort.

Despite only having one practice session due to it being a Sprint event, Lawson went on to make Q3 and finish the Dutch GP in seventh.

By having the traditional format in Monza, Lawson is expecting a less stressful event and more time to settle into the RB22.

Discussing what his mindset is going into the weekend, Lawson replied: "Just try and make the most of it. Again, I think, yeah, obviously, it's an interesting position for me to be in.

"And Zandvoort was, yeah, I mean, being a Sprint weekend is obviously quite stressful at times, but overall it was a good weekend.

"And at least now I've had that, you know, it should be a bit easier to adjust. We also have three practice sessions here. It's a much more normal weekend. So, yeah, it's another good opportunity."

title: The F1 rookies taking part in Italian GP FP1
excerpt:
Four rookie drivers will get behind the wheel of an F1 car at Monza this Friday, as teams continue to fulfil their mandatory obligations for the 2026 season.

Under current regulations, each team must run a rookie driver, defined as someone with no more than two grand prix starts, in FP1 on four occasions per season, twice per car.

With the Italian Grand Prix approaching, four teams have opted to use the Monza weekend to tick off part of that requirement.

Ayumu Iwasa will step into Max Verstappen's Red Bull RB22. The Japanese driver is no stranger to FP1 duties, having accumulated seven such outings since 2024 with both Red Bull and Racing Bulls.

Luke Browning, a Williams Academy product with six previous FP1 appearances to his name, will replace Alex Albon in the FW48.

Alpine's Paul Aron, who has already racked up eight FP1 sessions split between Audi and Alpine in 2025, takes over Pierre Gasly's A526.

But perhaps the most intriguing name is Colton Herta, the American IndyCar star who will drive Sergio Perez's Cadillac for his third FP1 outing of 2026, having made his debut in the format at Barcelona earlier this season.

title: Lando Norris raises McLaren concern as biggest weakness set for ultimate exposure
excerpt:
Lando Norris has raised concerns that Monza will expose McLaren’s key weakness in chicanes and general low-speed corners at this weekend’s Italian Grand Prix.

Norris enters the event full of confidence, with momentum firmly behind him after securing back-to-back victories either side of the summer break in Hungary and the Netherlands.

This has seen him move to within 83 points of championship leader Kimi Antonelli and left many believing that the defending world champion could yet be a title contender once again.

However, Monza is a circuit that is not expected to be as strong for the Woking-based outfit as the recent rounds, largely due to the style of corners.

McLaren has struggled in chicanes and slow-speed corners since the start of the new power-unit regulations, something of which Monza has several.

It is a legendary venue boasting high-speed straights, followed by heavy braking and tight chicanes, with Norris conceding that the papaya squad does not have an immediate fix.

Asked if McLaren has a fix for its chicane and slow speed corner weakness, Norris told select media, including RacingNews365: "No, there’s not a lot we can do, really.

"It’s just that every car has strengths and weaknesses and is designed in slightly different ways, and ours is just not quite where we want it to be in that style of corner and at that speed. But clearly, we are also able to extract more performance in other types of corners.

"So it’s just the style of F1 that everyone has kind of strengths and weaknesses. It’s obviously something we acknowledge, which is a good thing, and we’re trying to work on it as quickly as possible. Sometimes things can be quick in F1, sometimes not.

"So it’s stuff that the whole team is working on back at the factory, and it’s more just that there’s clear acknowledgement that this has been our biggest weakness lately, and we know that we might struggle again here in those styles of corners."

Compromising high-speed performance

McLaren’s real hope of being strong in the slow-speed corners this weekend would be to compromise its top speed.

It is a decision Norris and the team will have to make, although the Briton has recognised that it is not a change which will guarantee an improvement.

"So we’ll see what we can do to maybe compromise a little bit on the high speed to try and get something in the slow speed," added Norris.

"But if it were simple, we would do a lot more of it. So it’s not as simple as simply doing that at the same time. So, yeah, we’ll see. We know it’s a place we have to work on."

title: Charles Leclerc confirms Lewis Hamilton Ferrari 'priority' at Italian GP
excerpt:
Charles Leclerc has stated that Lewis Hamilton has “priority” over where to place his car in the queue this weekend at the Italian Grand Prix.

The Monza F1 track contains several long straights, making it one of the fastest tracks on the schedule.

Slipstreaming has been an important factor in extracting lap time around the venue, but it is set to be even more prominent this weekend due to the new-for-2026 power units, which will likely see the cars lose speed at the end of straights as the battery depletes.

In qualifying, cars will be chasing any slipstream they can to punch a hole in the air and reduce drag - and for Hamilton, he may find it easier than his team-mate.

“For the slipstream, we've always had the same philosophy over the years, where one time Lewis has the priority to choose where he wants to start, and one weekend it's on me,” Leclerc told media including RacingNews365.

“This weekend, Lewis will have the priority, so I guess we'll go for a slipstream.

“Whether we are going to compromise one qualifying [for] the other, I don't think that will happen.

“If we can help each other, trying to start the lap at the optimum distance between each other, that will be done.

“I'll try to find another slipstream off someone else, hoping to put myself in the best possible place.”

On Sunday, it is anticipated that there will be a return of 'yo-yo racing', which was a common feature during the early season grands prix.

When asked if it will be equally as important to work with his team-mate during the race as it is in qualifying, Leclerc said: ”For the race, that is a very valid point.

“We've started to look at it now for quite a few days and trying to understand.

“It's also very, very difficult to predict because the thing is that once you are in the car, it always looks nice from outside.

“But the difference is sometimes that much that it is very difficult to react to the car in front.

“It's not that you can avoid yo-yo racing if you end up in a situation like this, but we'll try to do the best possible job and try to do better.”

title: Fernando Alonso sets clear parameters over uncertain F1 future
excerpt:
Fernando Alonso has outlined what will keep him racing in F1 next season, with the Aston Martin driver yet to put pen to paper on a new deal with the Silverstone-based squad.

3 September 5:15PM

Fernando Alonso has said he will not remain in F1 simply to fight at the lower end of the points, as uncertainty continues over his future beyond the current season.

The Aston Martin driver is under contract until the end of the current campaign, but has repeatedly indicated this year that he is assessing whether he wants to continue in the championship.

Speaking ahead of the Italian Grand Prix at Monza, Alonso made clear that his decision will depend on more than Aston Martin's immediate performance level.

Asked whether battling for eighth, ninth or tenth would be enough to persuade him to stay, Alonso replied: "No."

And when asked in follow-up if he would only continue if there was more at stake, he added: "Yes."

The comments come during a difficult campaign for Aston Martin, who sit tenth in the constructors' championship after 12 rounds. Alonso has scored all three of the team's points so far, while Lance Stroll is yet to finish in the top 10.

The Silverstone-based squad has struggled for consistency throughout the season, with 11 retirements across both cars and only two points finishes.

However, the team showed signs of progress at Zandvoort, where Alonso recovered from P18 on the grid to finish ninth.

The result tripled Alonso's points tally for the season and followed a series of updates introduced since Budapest.

While the Spaniard said the performance suggested Aston Martin's development direction was improving, he stressed that ninth place could not be treated as a major success.

"We cannot be happy with just P9, and I think no one is happy in the team," Alonso told media, including RacingNews365. "It was a nice boost for everyone, knowing that at least the direction that we are taking is the right one, because we changed a lot of things on the car since Budapest, and obviously we know, or we feel, that in the corners we are getting to a much better place.

"So that gives hope for everyone in Silverstone that if we keep on going with this philosophy and this strategy and this pace of development, eventually we will be one of the fastest in the corners; so we tick one of the boxes."

Driver

Fernando Alonso

Spanish

14

Alonso points to regulations as key factor

Aston Martin's progress has not been limited to chassis development. The team has also been working through issues with Honda's power unit after a difficult start to the new partnership, with vibration and drivability problems affecting performance.

Alonso said Monza would provide a clearer picture of any gains because of the circuit's heavy emphasis on straight-line speed, but he was cautious about the latest step after Zandvoort.

"Then, on the engine side, I think Zandvoort was not a big improvement, to be honest," Alonso added. "The drivability was a problem, and the extra power was difficult to feel in Zandvoort.

"Maybe Monza is going to be a truer test for the engine, but still a long way to go, and we need to improve at both ends, on chassis and on engine for next year; it's a must. So that's the biggest thing."

Although Aston Martin's competitiveness remains a significant part of the wider picture, Alonso said his own decision will be influenced heavily by the direction of Formula 1's regulations.

The two-time F1 drivers' champion has been critical of the new rules throughout the season, arguing that the current generation of cars has placed too much emphasis on energy management and reduced the role of driver input.

He previously claimed after the British Grand Prix that "no driver talent" was needed, and said in Monaco that the cars were the worst he had driven at the circuit.

Asked at Monza how those concerns would affect his future, Alonso said he would continue to give his maximum regardless of Aston Martin's position, but suggested the wider direction of the sport remains a concern.

"And for my decision, it's not really about the car," he said. "I will be professional and working at my 100 per cent, fighting for P15 or fighting for a podium, but for me it's more about the regulations.

"Unfortunately, it's what it is. This is not the Formula 1 we grew up with, and this is not the Formula 1 that we all want, drivers, spectators.

"So we must change a few things. It will not happen immediately. It will happen for the future. But I hope I can contribute somehow to the next set of regulations, [and] we go back to the real Formula 1."

title: Max Verstappen provides health update after battling 'awful' illness
excerpt:
Max Verstappen has shared how he is feeling ahead of the Italian Grand Prix, having suffered through illness at the previous round in Zandvoort.

Max Verstappen has confirmed he is fully recovered from the illness that plagued him throughout the Dutch Grand Prix, describing his experience as "awful" in the days before and after the race.

The Red Bull driver was visibly under the weather across the entire Zandvoort weekend, battling flu-like symptoms that left him feeling far from his best.

He qualified seventh for his home race and then saw his afternoon end abruptly on the opening lap when he lost control at the banked final corner on a damp track, spinning hard into the barriers and triggering a red flag.

Speaking to media ahead of the Italian Grand Prix at Monza, Verstappen was asked how he had been feeling in the days after Zandvoort, addressing both the first-lap crash and his illness.

"I felt good in terms of the impact, because it was the SAFER [steel and foam energy reduction] barrier," the Dutchman told media, including RacingNews365.

"So that was the first time that I did that. It actually did its job really well."

Driver

Max Verstappen

Dutch

3

'The whole week in Zandvoort was awful'

While the four-time F1 drivers' champion walked away from the crash unscathed, it was the illness that proved far harder to shake off.

The 28-year-old admitted that the bug lingered well beyond the race weekend itself.

The week-long break between the Dutch and Italian rounds afforded Verstappen the time he needed to get back to full fitness.

"But yeah, I was very ill," the 71-time grand prix winner added. "You appreciate it once you're fully healed, like how good it is to feel like that, because the whole week in Zandvoort was awful.

"And even after Zandvoort, for a few days, I was still not good. So it was actually really nice to have that week to recover and feel better again, because it's been a very long time since I felt like that."

title: Kimi Antonelli confirms Mercedes discussions in George Russell support role
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli has confirmed that talks have been held with Mercedes ahead of this weekend's Italian Grand Prix regarding him supporting George Russell.

The championship leader faces the task of starting his home race from the back of the grid, with the Silver Arrows choosing to fit Antonelli's car with an entirely new power unit.

Antonelli was already on the cusp of a grid drop due to having almost used every engine component within his pool, something he has now exceeded.

Monza was chosen as the best place to take a heavy grid penalty by the Brackley-based operation, due to the expectation that overtaking will be very possible.

It makes qualifying effectively meaningless for Antonelli, with his title rivals having a great chance to reduce the 20-year-old's title advantage.

One of those drivers is Russell, who Antonelli has confirmed he will support in qualifying by offering a tow should the instruction come from Mercedes.

Asked if helping Russell has been discussed with the team, Antonelli told select media, including RacingNews365: "Yeah, it is.

"It has been discussed with the team, and yes, we have agreed on a few things, so let's see how the session develops. But if the team asks me to do so, I will do it.

"I will do it because, yeah, obviously, I will still be happy to get pole, but of course, I'm starting at the back.

"So, if I could do anything to help the team, I will. I will do it."

title: Lewis Hamilton details 'sheer magnitude' of Italian GP pressure as clear target set
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton has set his sights on winning the Italian Grand Prix for the first time as a Ferrari driver this weekend.

The seven-time champion has enjoyed huge success at Monza, winning five times in his career - the joint-most alongside Michael Schumacher.

However, his last win at the venue came eight years ago, while Ferrari has won twice since then with Charles Leclerc, in 2019 and 2024.

Ferrari arrive at the Italian GP this weekend with an upgraded engine as it hopes to get involved in the fight at the front - a mission Hamilton has full faith in.

“I strongly believe that the team has what it takes to win at this level, how close it is at the front,” Hamilton told media including RacingNews365.

“For us to win this weekend, and at any weekend, it takes the whole collective to come together. It's not just one thing; everything has to flow from the beginning.

“And I really thought coming into this weekend, just thinking of the sheer magnitude of the concept that I'm coming to this grand prix... I didn't even know that I was equal with Michael on wins.

“But the thought of that there is a first ahead of me, in a sense of potentially, if you were to win, you go into new territory.

“Winning in Monza for the first time with Ferrari is something I've witnessed Charles win in 2019 when I was on the podium with him.

“To do it while I'm here would be phenomenal. The thought of if I did do that, probably will be the only black driver to ever do that for Ferrari in Italy, probably in history.

“A lot of those thoughts have been through my mind.”

Hamilton has taken to the top step of the podium with Ferrari once already this year, triumphing in Barcelona in emotional circumstances.

A win at Monza would likely match or even exceed the excitement that was felt in June, and Hamilton is feeling the tension rising as he prepares for the first day of on-track action.

“The pressure is high, you want to deliver for the team,” he said.

“All those people at the factory, many of them will get to come to this race. The Tifosi come out in huge numbers, the passion is unmatched, and you want to deliver for them as well.

“And my mum's here this weekend, I don't think she's been to Monza, but also particularly on a Ferrari weekend.

“I wanted her to experience that and bring any of the lucky dust she can bring.”

title: Franco Colapinto highlights F1 'goal' after fresh Alpine deal
excerpt:
Franco Colapinto has outlined his latest F1 goal after securing a drive on the 2027 grid with Alpine.

The deal was announced last week, with Alpine opting to retain an unchanged line-up by keeping Colapinto alongside Pierre Gasly, who is secured on a long-term deal.

Colapinto joined Alpine last year after replacing Jack Doohan just a handful of rounds into the season.

It was a tormenting campaign for the Enstone-based squad as it placed its resources into its 2026 challenger, which has been a regular point-scorer this year.

Colapinto's performances aided the team's decision to keep him for another year, and the Argentine pledged to continue to play his part in pushing the team forward.

“Of course, very happy to continue - very, very happy and grateful to the team that has done an amazing job since I started,“ Colapinto told media including RacingNews365.

“Last year was tricky, this year we have made a big step together as a team, and it's great to continue this journey together and to be able to keep working as a family for next season.

“We have a lot of work to do, and we are going to try hard to keep developing and keep improving as a team, that's the goal for us.”

In contrast to its approach last year, Colapinto has suggested Alpine will not halt the development of its current car in a bid to start next year's campaign in an even stronger position.

As it targets a top five finishing position for the first time since 2022, Colapinto insisted its goal is to end the year as high as it can in the standings.

“It's great to be with the team for another year,” he added. “Of course, we have to keep working a lot.

“We are going to be pushing this year. First, our goal isto finish as high as we can, and then, of course, we want another step for 2027.”

title: Max Verstappen sets fresh Red Bull target after 'disappointing' moment
excerpt:
Max Verstappen has stated that both he and Red Bull must work to ensure the RB22 is fine-tuned to a competitive window at the Italian Grand Prix this weekend.

The Monza Circuit hosts the 13th round of the 2026 F1 campaign this weekend, with Verstappen seeking a return to the podium.

After back-to-back top-three results in Belgium and Hungary, the four-time champion entered his home event in the Netherlands last time out hoping to add to his podium tally.

However, his race ended on the opening lap as he spun in tricky conditions, making heavy contact with the barrier.

It marked an excruciating result for Verstappen, at what was the final Dutch Grand Prix for the foreseeable future.

“Not being able to finish the race in Zandvoort was disappointing,” Verstappen said ahead of the weekend.

“But it was still really special to see the fans at the circuit one last time and thank them for all the memories.”

Verstappen has triumphed at the Italian Grand Prix at Monza on three occasions during his career, including last year's event as he continued to close the gap to McLaren in the championship.

However, the 28-year-old refrained from putting a label on expectations for the weekend ahead, insisting the primary task was getting the car set up in a strong window.

“We are heading to Monza, after a reset, and it is difficult to predict how competitive we will be there,” he said.

“There are a few things we need to work on to be a bit closer to the pace and to make sure balance of the car is right.

“Monza is one of my favourite tracks and I like that it is an old-school, fast circuit; I always enjoy coming here and seeing the passionate fans.

“It is a track that we have typically performed well at before so we will wait and see what is possible."

title: Key F1 supplier 'braking' ground as new challenge intensifies
excerpt:
F1’s new era has presented a serious challenge for Brembo, the brake manufacturer partnering with all Formula 1 teams, while significant preparations are also required for 2027. The Italian company's research, development, and testing department is working at full throttle — all under one roof.

3 September 12:45PM

Preparing for F1's new era, which started this season, was a massive task for Brembo, because braking has become more complex than ever before at the pinnacle of motorsport.

Now, it demands continuous action from the brake manufacturer, connected to all teams, who must simultaneously focus on 2027 whilst meeting the demands of this year.

During an exclusive interview with RacingNews365, Andrea Dellavedova, race engineer for the Italian brand, pointed out that changing the combustion-to-electric power ratio and the timing of the decision intensifies the challenge for Brembo as well.

"Yeah, because now we have done half a year, so we understand more, and we were focusing on some direction. As next year the energy ratio will change, what we learned this year will not be that useful for the new development," he begins.

"This year we already started to think about the 2027 braking system, but now we have to think newly about the system, and we cannot use all the info that we discovered this year for the next one."

As is well known, after lengthy and extensive consultations, the FIA confirmed in June that it will modify the ratio in two steps: it will change to 58:42 for 2027, and then shift to 60:40 for 2028.

"Being in a very fast environment, the more time we have to develop the new system, the better it is. If the communication would happen some weeks before… it's always easier, because we have to design and test the prototype, and then launch the production," Dellavedova adds.

"The time horizon is very short, because the teams need the components for early next year. It's something that takes time, both designing and producing our components. From the design to the production phase, it takes months; it's not something that you can do in weeks, because the process itself of producing the disc and the carbon material is very long, because they have to spend time in the oven, with several processes.

"Also, the calliper itself, they have to spend a lot of time on the machine. Then there is also the testing. Sometimes we do the testing and the production in parallel."

Brembo building on a strong foundation

The task is massive, but Brembo has a strong foundation to build upon: the brand's excellent engineers utilise state-of-the-art infrastructure.

The company's operational and administrative center is located in Kilometro Rosso, Bergamo's science and technology park, while they operate manufacturing and commercial facilities in 18 countries worldwide.

In terms of F1 and motorsport, Curno in Italy, located near the headquarters, is the key plant: this is where the racing technology is created.

"We have several dyno test benches that we use to test the new developments in terms of both materials, geometries and also dimensions of the braking system. They are running 24 hours per day, 6 days per week," says Dellavedova about the "witch's kitchen" in Curno.

According to the Italian engineer, keeping research, design, and development in-house and under one roof provides a major competitive advantage, even in the world of brake development.

"The performance is there with both offices and also the production and testing department," he continues.

"We are very close, so the designer can work on the laptop, design the new component and in a very fast way they just go to the first floor — the dyno test benches are there with the people working directly on the tests, so they have a very fast way of communicating, and also they can physically inspect the products that they are developing."

Although preparing for 2027 is a serious challenge for Brembo, Dellavedova looks to the future with confidence based on their current situation, available capacity, and experience.

He concludes: "In terms of timing, we are in line. In terms of performance, based on our experience, yes, because, of course, we are doing the best that we think will be the best for the next year."

title: Major F1 record predicted to be broken at Italian GP
excerpt:
Aston Martin's chief trackside officer Mike Krack has stated he is expecting a large amount of overtaking at the Italian Grand Prix this weekend.

The 54-year-old went so far as to say that it could set a new record for the highest number of passes in a single race.

The current record was set at the 2023 Dutch Grand Prix, which saw 186 position changes throughout the field during a chaotic event impacted by rain.

This year's F1 cars race somewhat differently compared to challengers from the past, with energy deployment playing a major role following the increase in battery output.

Across the opening events of the year, it was common for cars to be repassed shortly after completing a move due to running out of energy.

With Monza's layout featuring many long straights which could see a repeat of such a situation, Krack is expecting to see many overtakes take place on Sunday.

“It will be an interesting exercise to validate your models, but also to see how operationally you manage it,” Krack told media including RacingNews365.

“It is one side to say the effect big or small, but also you have to be in a position to follow someone.

“So there are quite a lot of restrictions on the energy side this weekend. It will be interesting to see how teams we we go about it, first of all, in free-of-tow deployment, but then also in a tow situation.

“Then also in the race, how easy passing will be, and especially the passing and repassing games. It probably will be a record of all time here, or like MotoGP.”

Monza sits as one of the fastest F1 tracks on the race calendar, with speeds peaking at around 360 km/h in modern times - however, the figures are set to decrease this year.

Should drivers use different energy deployment strategies throughout the upcoming event, Krack admits that it could create a dangerous situation.

“Normally, the deployment profiles converge over a weekend, so I do not expect any major differences.

“But if people deploy completely differently, then there is always a risk.”

title: F1 teams handed 'crucify' warning as Ferrari singled out
excerpt:
Mika Hakkinen has addressed the team orders situation in F1 after the issue came to the fore at Zandvoort.

3 September 11:15AM

Mika Hakkinen has warned F1 teams that fans will turn on them if they impose team orders to shape the title fight, singling out Ferrari's handling of Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc at the Dutch Grand Prix as a case study in indecision.

Mercedes executed a clean driver swap at Zandvoort, instructing George Russell to let Kimi Antonelli through for second place after a late Virtual Safety Car had artificially inverted their positions.

Antonelli, on fresher soft tyres, had been running ahead before the pit sequence and was the faster car. Russell questioned the call but complied; Mercedes locked out second and third behind race winner Lando Norris, and the matter was largely put to bed.

Ferrari's situation was messier. Hamilton, on a better strategy and fresher rubber, caught Leclerc in the middle phase of the race and asked to be let through, but the Scuderia never issued the order.

Instead, the team eventually pitted Leclerc to clear Hamilton's path, but the delay cost Hamilton several seconds, and he finished fourth, less than a second behind Russell, costing him a podium finish. Hamilton was frustrated, suggesting Ferrari should learn from Mercedes' decisiveness.

Hakkinen, speaking to Sky Sports F1, made clear he understood Hamilton's reaction and felt it went beyond mere frustration.

"I think what Lewis experienced in Zandvoort, it was explained from the team why it happened," the two-time F1 drivers' champion said. "Emotions with Lewis' experience were absolutely normal. Maybe it wasn't only emotion, just also common sense, 'We can score more points if you let me overtake!'"

Hakkinen also offered a broader explanation for why drivers so often clash with their teams in these moments, pointing to the information gap between the cockpit and the pit wall.

"But nowadays when I look at grand prix racing from the outside, when I'm in the paddock, it's different. You see much more, you get much more information on what's happening," he said.

"The drivers are getting only a very tiny percentage of the information we get on TV, so when they are following another car, and it doesn't let them overtake, they don't have the information and the calculations that the team have, so then very often you get these kinds of reactions from the drivers, which is very normal."

Driver

Mika Häkkinen

Finnish

A warning for the title fight

It is a nuance that helps explain Hamilton's visible frustration at Zandvoort. Sitting behind Leclerc, aware only that he was faster and losing time, he could not see the broader strategic picture Ferrari was attempting to manage.

That context does not excuse the team's hesitation, Hakkinen suggested, but it does put the driver's reaction into perspective.

The 20-time grand prix winner drew on his own era racing against Michael Schumacher's Ferrari to illustrate how much the sport has changed, and why teams face a far more combustible environment when it comes to managing two drivers.

"The fanbase has changed in Formula 1; the generation is different than in my time," Hakkinen said. "When I was racing against Michael Schumacher when he was at Ferrari, they started doing team orders already at the first race of the season.

"It was very obvious that if one driver is very strong in a team and started to win races and score points, the team is very much aware that if they want to win the world championship, they need to support this one driver 100 per cent.

"That's what Michael Schumacher was able to manage to do with Ferrari when he was racing there.

"We had a little bit of a different philosophy at McLaren. We wanted to give both drivers the same opportunity until the points were at a point that one couldn't catch the other; then the team-mate has to start supporting the leading driver. That was a common-sense operation."

With the championship battle tightening, Hakkinen's central message was clear: the old playbook no longer applies cleanly.

Teams cannot simply install a number one and a number two without consequence, because the modern fanbase will not accept it quietly.

"Now the teams want to win the drivers' championship and the constructors' championship; they want to win both. So it's important that both drivers are getting maximum performance all the time in every race...," he said.

"Which team is going to do this kind of change [implementing team orders], and what are the arguments they are going to give and tell the fans? This is going to be an important factor.

"All these drivers have a huge fanbase these days in the world, and if the team are going to decide one day that this driver is going to be number two, the fans are going to crucify this team."

title: Lando Norris traits highlighted where 'he has improved the most'
excerpt:
McLaren team principal Andrea Stella has highlighted two of the key areas where he feels Lando Norris has improved significantly after thrusting himself back into the picture for this season's F1 drivers' title.

Following a major upgrade on the MCL40 ahead of the Hungarian Grand Prix, Norris has ended his winless drought with back-to-back victories either side of the summer break at the Hungaroring and Zandvoort.

From barely being mentioned as a title contender, Norris is back in the conversation, albeit the Briton still faces a considerable task if he is to retain his championship as he currently trails leader Kimi Antonelli by 83 points.

From Stella's perspective, however, he has enjoyed a different side to Norris of late, in particular after he gave himself a rare pat on the back for his part in achieving victory in the Dutch Grand Prix. Ordinarily, he has been quick to self-criticise.

One of the highlights of Norris' performance was his pass on Antonelli around the outside of Turn 1, notably with Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton also in the equation.

"I would say he is definitely expressing a higher level of assertiveness as he drives," said Stella, speaking to the media, including RacingNews365. "The manoeuvre to pass Antonelli was a really good demonstration of that.

"He is demonstrating more self-confidence, and with self-confidence, it is interesting, and I quite like it.

"Sometimes, self-confidence is not demonstrated by being the most aggressive. Sometimes you are self-confident when you think, 'You know what? I'm not going to fight now because I might lose this fight. It's a very long race. See you at the end of the race'.

"It's this confidence in your means, in your strength that I quite like, which means that sometimes you are the one backing off when the situation becomes too risky. So I do see the self-confidence.

"We need to remember that in both of the last couple of races that he won, he didn't defend the pole position. He was actually second at the end of the first lap.

"But I did not perceive any decay in his confidence. Instead, he was fast and just preparing his opportunity to then cash in on his competitiveness.

"So I think assertiveness and confidence are probably the two characteristics where he has improved the most from a non-technical, non-operational point of view."

Next up for McLaren and Norris is the Italian Grand Prix at Monza on September 6.

title: Ferrari handed 'cautiously optimistic' verdict as Monza pressure cooker awaits
excerpt:
Former IndyCar driver James Hinchcliffe has handed Ferrari and its fans his belief that the Scuderia can be "cautiously optimistic" about this weekend's Italian Grand Prix.

F1's annual visit to Monza represents the biggest weekend of Ferrari's season, with it being the ultimate pressure-cooker event for the Maranello-based outfit.

Ferrari consistently introduces an upgrade package especially for its home race, in pursuit of securing victory at one of the most iconic races on the calendar.

With Ferrari having failed to claim a podium in the last two races, there will be pressure on the team to return to the rostrum at the very least, if not challenge for victory.

A special livery has already been unveiled by Ferrari, while the Italian manufacturer is also introducing its second engine upgrade of the year in pursuit of Mercedes.

Ferrari, and in particular Lewis Hamilton, do remain in the title fight, although a strong result is needed this weekend to keep genuine hopes alive.

Predicting whether Ferrari will perform strongly or not has been a challenge in 2026, with it often performing well at venues where it is expected to struggle, and then doing badly where it is expected to thrive.

Discussing Ferrari's chances this weekend, Hinchcliffe told the F1 Nation podcast: "Well, it's interesting, right? Because they've been competitive at tracks that maybe we weren't expecting them to be, and then vice versa, maybe a little bit off the pace at some tracks that we kind of thought they were going to be right up front.

"I think of Silverstone and even Spa. They were decent, and you're heading to Monza, a big horsepower track. They seem to have found something in that department.

"They always seem to have a little bit of something special there, don't they? I mean, they are usually competitive. Even in seasons when they're not that competitive in other places, they seem to focus.

"It's like they build their car around Monza, and then, okay, we'll figure the rest out as we go. So, I mean, cautiously optimistic for the Tifosi that they can have a strong weekend. Again, they didn't qualify particularly well at Spa, if I remember, but they were decent in the race."
